web_title: 1. Origin, Corporate Evolution & Past Operational Cycles
book_title: Chapter 1: From Rajkot Job-Shop Lathes to Defence-Grade CNC Platforms
question: How did a 2003 Rajkot lathe workshop evolve into a 2,500-machine CNC manufacturer, and what do its past revenue and margin cycles reveal about its structural resilience?

epigraph.quote: In capital goods, the factory you build during the quiet years determines how much of the upcycle you actually capture.
epigraph.author: Industrial Underwriting Maxim

web_blocks.html: Macpower CNC Machines Limited was incorporated in 2003 at Metoda GIDC near Rajkot, Gujarat. First-generation entrepreneur Rupesh J. Mehta founded the firm alongside co-promoters and family members [13, 14]. Rajkot's industrial belt—known for diesel engines, castings, bearings, and auto-ancillary shops—gave Macpower both local buyers and skilled machinists. For its first decade, Macpower built conventional and entry-level CNC lathes under the 'Turner' brand [13, 15]. It served MSMEs with a modest capacity of roughly 600 machines per year [13, 15]. During that pre-listing phase, the company operated like a classic assembly shop. It bought sheet-metal enclosures, spindles, and control panels from outside vendors. As a result, operating profit margins (OPM) stayed in the low single digits: 2.5% in FY15, 3.4% in FY16, and 2.4% in FY17 on flat sales of ₹64–68 Cr [1, 15].

The structural shift began with Macpower's 2018 Initial Public Offering on the NSE Emerge platform [13]. Many SME issuers used IPO cash to pay promoter debt or plug working capital gaps. Instead, Macpower put almost all of its ₹39 Cr net inflow into backward integration and capacity doubling at its 8-acre Metoda plant [1, 5, 13]. Between FY18 and FY21, management built in-house sheet-metal fabrication, powder-coating lines, and precision spindle machining [5, 15]. Those additions lifted annual capacity from 600 machines to roughly 1,300 machines [5, 15]. The financial payoff came fast. Operating margins jumped from 2.4% in FY17 to 11% in FY18 and 12% in FY19, while revenue more than doubled from ₹68 Cr to ₹140 Cr [1].

To judge Macpower without looking at its stock quote, we must study how it performed across three industrial cycles from FY15 to H1 FY27 [1, 15]. The first test was the FY18–FY20 domestic auto and NBFC slowdown, followed by the March 2020 COVID-19 shock. Revenue fell 42% from ₹140 Cr in FY19 to ₹82 Cr in FY20 [1]. Operating profit dropped from ₹17 Cr to ₹5 Cr as OPM narrowed from 12% to 6%, and ROCE sank from 30% to 6% [1]. Yet Macpower never posted an annual operating loss or net loss. Net profit stayed positive at ₹3 Cr in FY20, and debt remained tiny at ₹1 Cr because management had avoided debt during the 2018 expansion [1].

The second cycle (FY21–FY23) tested Macpower's post-COVID rebound and supply-chain resilience. Revenue recovered 38% to ₹113 Cr in FY21 and surged 68% to ₹190 Cr in FY22 [1]. Growth then slowed to 6% in FY23 (₹202 Cr) as global chip and controller shortages at FANUC and Siemens delayed machine dispatches [1]. Even so, operating margins held steady in an 8%–11% band across FY21–FY23 [1]. That stability proved that the 2018 backward integration had permanently raised Macpower's trough margin floor above its pre-IPO 2.5%–3.4% range [1]. During this cycle, Macpower also launched its 'NEXA' vertical. NEXA is a dedicated sales and engineering arm for Vertical Machining Centers (VMCs), Horizontal Machining Centers (HMCs), Vertical Turret Lathes (VTLs), and Double Column Machines aimed at replacing imports [4, 8, 15].

The third and ongoing cycle (FY24–H1 FY27) marks Macpower's shift from a cyclical shop supplier to a multi-vertical precision platform [5, 15]. Revenue grew 19% to ₹241 Cr in FY24, 9% to ₹262 Cr in FY25, and 27% to ₹333 Cr in FY26 [1, 2]. Operating margins expanded to 15% in FY24 and 16% in both FY25 and FY26 [1, 2]. In Q2 FY27 (ended September 2026), quarterly revenue hit a record ₹120.33 Cr (+40.4% YoY), lifting H1 FY27 revenue to ₹215.56 Cr [4, 15]. In November 2025, a 40,000 sq ft assembly addition raised Metoda capacity by 500 units to 2,500 machines, which now runs near 95% utilization [4, 9, 15]. Meanwhile, the pending order book grew 2.7x in three years to ₹476.7 Cr by September 2026, with NEXA making up 40% of the backlog [4, 15].

web_blocks.takeaway: Macpower's structural margin floor stepped up from ~3% pre-IPO to 6% in the FY20 trough and 16%+ at high utilization, proving that backward integration and product-mix premiumization altered its unit economics—though revenue remains inherently tied to industrial capex cycles [1, 15].

web_blocks.title: Governance & Promoter Continuity Check
paragraphs: Macpower has zero subsidiaries, so its standalone financials represent 100% of the business [2, 15]. Promoter ownership held steady at 73.17%–73.22% from December 2023 through September 2026, with zero equity dilution since the 2018 IPO [1, 4].

Top leadership has stayed intact for over two decades. Rupesh Mehta (CMD) brings 29+ years of machine-tool experience, CEO Nikesh Mehta runs execution, and CFO Rajnikant Raja has served on the Board since April 2004 [14, 15].

From FY24 to FY26, Macpower funded ₹9.16 Cr, ₹12.42 Cr, and ₹15.36 Cr of annual capex strictly from internal cash flow. Total debt stayed at ₹1–3 Cr, while the firm paid modest dividends (₹1.50/share recommended for FY26) [1, 15].

book_paragraphs: If you and I walked onto the shop floor of Metoda GIDC on the outskirts of Rajkot in 2003, we would not have seen a futuristic robotics lab. We would have seen a modest, determined machine-tool workshop started by Rupesh Mehta, building basic 'Turner' brand lathes for the hundreds of small auto-component and casting job shops clustered across Gujarat. For its first fourteen years, Macpower CNC Machines Limited was a classic Indian SME assembler. It bought sheet-metal covers, spindles, and electrical panels from outside vendors, bolted them together, and sold machines for thin, single-digit operating margins—just 2.4% to 3.4% between FY15 and FY17 on flat revenues of ₹64 to ₹68 crore.

Why does that early history matter so much today? Because it gives you a clean baseline for what an un-integrated Indian CNC assembler earns. When you buy all your sub-assemblies from third-party job shops, you are essentially a contract integrator with zero pricing power. Your gross margin is dictated by vendor quotes, and any dip in factory volume wipes out your operating profit. Between FY15 and FY17, Macpower's net profit was barely ₹0 to ₹1 crore a year, and its return on capital employed fluctuated wildly from 8% to 19%.

What separates a durable industrial compounder from a permanent job-shop assembler is what management does with its first real windfall of capital. When Macpower listed on the NSE Emerge platform in 2018, it raised ₹39 crore. Instead of using that cash to pay down promoter loans or speculate in unrelated businesses, Mehta poured it straight back into the Metoda plant. Between 2018 and 2021, Macpower built its own sheet-metal fabrication line, its own powder-coating facility, and its own precision spindle-machining shop. Capacity doubled from 600 machines a year to 1,300, and operating margins jumped from 2.4% in FY17 to 11% in FY18 and 12% in FY19 as revenues climbed from ₹68 crore to ₹140 crore.

Now, you might ask: did that backward integration magically cure cyclicality? Not at all—and the numbers from FY20 prove it. When the domestic auto slowdown collided with the COVID-19 lockdowns in March 2020, Macpower's sales plunged 42% in a single year, from ₹140 crore down to ₹82 crore. Operating profit fell from ₹17 crore to ₹5 crore, and return on capital employed sank from 30% to 6%. Yet look closely at what did not happen: Macpower did not bleed red ink, and it did not trip over bank covenants. Because it carried almost zero debt—just ₹1 crore of borrowings—it stayed profitable even at the bottom of a once-in-a-generation industrial freeze, posting ₹3 crore of net profit.

That survival instinct set up the next two chapters of Macpower's evolution. During the post-COVID rebound from FY21 to FY23, sales jumped from ₹113 crore to ₹202 crore, even though global semiconductor and CNC controller shortages from FANUC and Siemens temporarily capped FY23 growth at 6%. Crucially, operating margins held in an 8% to 11% band—roughly triple the pre-IPO trough—proving that in-house spindles and sheet metal had permanently raised the company's margin floor. At the same time, management used those years to launch NEXA, a dedicated engineering and sales vertical designed to build heavier, higher-precision machines capable of replacing expensive imports from Taiwan and Europe.

By FY24 through the first half of FY27, all of those quiet investments converged. Revenue rose to ₹241 crore in FY24, ₹262 crore in FY25, and ₹333 crore in FY26, while operating margins stepped up to 15% and then 16%. In November 2025, a 40,000-square-foot assembly addition lifted annual capacity from 2,000 to 2,500 machines, and by the September 2026 quarter, sales hit an all-time quarterly record of ₹120.33 crore—running the Metoda plant at 95% utilization against a ₹476.7 crore order book.

Equally important for you and me is how the promoters behaved throughout this climb. Macpower has zero subsidiaries, zero equity dilution since 2018, and a promoter family holding steady at 73.22%. Rupesh Mehta has been at the helm for over twenty-nine years in the machine-tool trade, Whole-Time Director and CEO Nikesh Mehta runs day-to-day execution, and CFO Rajnikant Raja has sat on the Board since 2004. The lesson is clear: Macpower's history is not a straight-line software story, but a twenty-three-year grind of incremental backward integration, conservative balance-sheet management, and deliberate climbing of the precision ladder—punctuated by sharp industrial downcycles whenever MSME customers pause their capex.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: When you study a capital-goods manufacturer, never judge it solely by its peak-cycle margin. Look at FY20, when Macpower's revenue fell 42% and it still posted a ₹3 crore net profit with negligible debt. That tells us the cost structure has real shock absorbers—even though demand itself remains unmistakably cyclical.
